trace.claim: The paper argues that online political hostility is associated with political engagement and its antecedents, contrary to theories that attribute hostility primarily to socioeconomic marginalization or personality-based factors.

The paper challenges the view that politically engaged users are only engaged in respectful or constructive dialogue, arguing instead that such engagement can be linked to more polarized and antagonistic behavior.

The paper opposes the idea that online political hostility is primarily driven by a small segment of users with extreme personality traits, suggesting instead that it is more broadly linked to political engagement.
Online political hostility is positively associated with indicators of political engagement and its antecedents.
Politically engaged users who express hostility are more active and have greater potential reach on X/Twitter.
The study uses a dataset combining panel survey data with online behavioral data from X (formerly Twitter).
The dataset includes 2,567 panelists whose survey responses were linked to their X handle.
The study scraped 9,250,180 posts from panelists between March 4, 2019, and January 2021.
Online political hostility is measured using a word embeddings approach called the Super-Unsupervised (SU) approach.
The SU approach calculates cosine similarity between individual posts and a 'political hate' word vector.
The study validates the SU measure through face validity, convergent and discriminant validity, criterion validity, external validity, and ecological validity.
The SU score is validated against 2,469 hand-labeled posts rated by four expert raters.
The study uses AFINN and Google Perspective API as secondary robustness measures for online hostility.
The study includes measures of political interest, political knowledge, education, internal efficacy, and political participation.
Online political hostility is positively associated with political interest, political knowledge, and online participation.
Users with higher levels of affective polarization show stronger associations between political engagement and online political hostility.
Politically hostile users post more frequently and have more friends and followers, indicating greater activity and potential reach.
The study finds that online political hostility is associated with political engagement and its antecedents, including education and internal efficacy.
The paper does not establish that political engagement causes online political hostility.
The paper does not claim that politically hostile users have formal network influence or centrality.
The paper does not provide evidence of a causal relationship between the different indicators of political engagement and their antecedents.
The paper does not directly test personality-based accounts centered on more antisocial traits such as Dark Triad traits, sadism, or other antagonistic traits.

The authors extend the revisionist perspective on political engagement by linking political engagement and its antecedents to online political hostility, moving beyond traditional explanations focused on deprivation or personality traits.
The paper disputes the claim that online political hostility is primarily driven by socioeconomic marginalization or personality-based factors like the Dark Triad.
